And 20% of clues, according to constructor, made by the NYT. Wow, wonder if that percentage goes down the more veteran and established the constructor. 

At, St. Ex...everyone knows him for The Little Prince. But Wind, Sand and Stars, his memoir of aviating on a mail route that took him to South America, all over Europe and north Africa, a crash in the Sahara -- is just as lovely a book, contemplative yet action-packed, with a different notion of what it means to be virile (MANLY):

“To be a man is, precisely, to be responsible. It is to feel shame at the sight of what seems to be unmerited misery. It is to take pride in a victory won by one's comrades. It is to feel, when setting one's stone, that one is contributing to the building of the world.”

Some might disagree with this, however:

“One cannot live any longer on refrigerators, on politics, on balance-sheets and cross-word puzzles. One cannot live any longer without poetry, color and love.”

Also, “Aimer, ce n'est pas se regarder l'un l'autre, c'est regarder ensemble dans la même direction.” (To love is not to look at one another, it is to look, together, in the same direction.)
I’m such a wiener I got too caught up thinking WEENIEROAST was wienerroast. Ach du lieber!

Gosh, this one was hard for me. 
I spent several minutes staring at VENAh wondering what it could possibly be, considering I was positive that 37D was hEDGE. (I may have misremembered what it meant to "hedge one's bets"). 
Overall though, it was a fun Tuesday that was definitely a good challenge for me! I learned VENAL, what a COATI is (hopefully I'll get to see one when I go to Peru with my Mom this May!!), and I added Raging Bull to my watchlist. Gotta love when you come away from a crossword knowing more than you did before. 
As an aside, I've felt recently like the tricky clues outlined in the column are not as reflective of the tricky clues in the puzzle! For example, other then the inclusion of "Hell" in the clue for 42A, I am very confused by SATAN. The cluing for ADOS and HAVANA (as I stated above, I'm not sure I totally understand it other than the vague idea of a Cuban cigar) also tripped me up. Comparing these clues to straightforward ones like 1D, 14A, or 27A (which were oddly included under Tricky Clues) it doesn't seem like Tricky Clues are truly the tricky clues! This is a little disappointing as I like to use the column as a tool for improving my solving and reading of clues. Just a suggestion for future columns!
Congrats to David Falkowski on his debut!!!
Hardest tuesday in quite a while, and sadly very Americana focused too. Had a very hard time.

Well, it looks as though the emus won't allow me to express my true feelings on how dispiriting this puzzle was for me.

I repeat, for me.  It seems no one else has noticed what seems to me to be blindingly obvious.

The cross of PALMAS and LEE was absolutely awful, as the L could have reasonably been any number of letters.  Worse, I've seen LEi far more often than LEE for Asian names.  

Beyond that, the spelling of WEENIE ROAST is awfully irregular--it seems the frankfurter can be spelled either as "wiener" or "weiner", but the word magically transforms into a double "e" word in the diminutive.  Utterly illogical.

I'm glad you got your debut puzzle, Mr. Falkowski, and I hope to see more from you in the future.

But this one was very much not for me.

I repeat, for me.

Congrats on the great debut!

Now I understand that that simply isn’t possible when making a crossword given how hard it is to make one, however I feel like that should be a factor that determines crossword difficulty. As someone who only plays Mondays and Tuesdays because I can usually solve them in a reasonable time, I was nowhere near able to complete this one. Frankly, it made me frustrated enough to make a comment for the first time.

The theme is a common Monday or Tuesday motif – what do the last words of the theme answers have in common?  It does have a subtle layer that I like: all the “kidding” words in the theme answers are nouns, but in their kidding sense they are verbs.

Nice touch, David.  Another nice touch was the Scrabbly-ness, with the grid just a Q short of a pangram.

ALL KIDDING ASIDE is just a gorgeous spanner smack in the center of the grid.

I also liked the alliterative [Pugilist’s pain point, perhaps] and was briefly and delightfully misdirected by [Big scoop], where I was trying to think of words for a reporter’s big scoop.

Some vagueness in the cluing and not-everyday answers (such as MOTO, FLAY, FAITA, VENAL GRANARY ARTES, and ORA) made me think, David, that you should try your hand at later-week puzzles.  In any case, this was a splendid outing for me.  Congratulations on your debut, and thank you!

All this talk about chickpeas:
We're so used to French *haricots verts*, Italian *salsa pomodoro*, and German *Kartoffelsalat*, that it's hard to imagine that, until the 16th c., none of those things existed--tomatoes, potatoes, and most beans are New World species. The only beans known to ancient and medieval Europeans were favas--which they consumed, gleefully, with chianti--chickpeas, and, if you include them, lentils. Chickpeas were known as "ciceres" to ancient Roman farmers, some of whom went on to become senators, with a gift for oratory. (So runs one theory for the origin of the cognomen "Cicero.")

This is an editing failure. It's one thing to have tough clues and esoteric answers, but to do those in the same section/crossing as an answer that's either never used or rarely used as a variant is not acceptable. There are a million ways to clue Havana

.

Andrzej, GARBANZO Etymology borrowed from Spanish (earlier usually garvanço), alteration (perhaps by blending with garroba "carob, algaroba" or gálbana "kind of pea") of earlier arvanço, ervanço, of uncertain origin Note: Recorded as arbānsuš or arbānšuš among Hispanic words in the Arabic pharmacopoeia Kitāb al-Mustaʻīnī of Yūsuf bin Isḥāq ibn Baklāriš (ca. 1106). As noted by Joan Coromines (Diccionario crítico etimológico castellano e hispánico), Greek erébinthos "chickpea" is unlikely to be the immediate source; the change i > a is ad hoc, and the outcome of -th- as z/ç is questionable. The initial arv-/erv- is comparable with a widespread group of words presumably of Mediterranean substratal origin—in addition to Greek erébinthos and órobos "the vetch Vicia ervilia," there are Latin ervum "the vetch Vicia ervilia," Germanic *arw(a)-(a)itō "pea" (whence Old High German araweiz, Old Saxon eriwit, erit, Old Norse ertr), Middle Irish orbaind "grains." The suffix of the Spanish word (*-antio?) is of obscure origin. https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/garbanzo
